Tidal locking occurs when a planet's orbital period matches its rotational period, causing one hemisphere to permanently face its star. This phenomenon, common among exoplanets orbiting close to red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme climate conditions in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the dramatic temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, bathed in perpetual starlight, can reach temperatures of hundreds of degrees, while the nightside plunges to frigid extremes where atmospheres may even freeze out.
